additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more persistent, non-bizarre or somewhat plausible delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked functional decline typical of schizophrenia. Outside the delusional themes, individuals often appear relatively intact, with preserved cognition, affect, and daily functioning, which can delay detection and treatment. Onset is typically in mid-to-late adulthood and may follow psychosocial stressors, interpersonal conflicts, or situations that can be misinterpreted and woven into a fixed false belief. It is distinguished from mood and psychotic disorders by the circumscribed nature of the beliefs, minimal other psychotic features, and relatively stable overall functioning.

patient.personality: Andrew is a meticulous, visually oriented and introspective professional who balances structured analytical work with solitary creative pursuits like painting, poetry, and gardening.
patient.stressor: About eighteen months ago, Andrew’s firm underwent a leadership change and began aggressively pushing new cost-cutting targets and tighter bidding timelines, placing intense scrutiny on his estimates and introducing a new project management system he privately doubted. A contentious hospital project, where several unexpected site conditions led to overruns, resulted in repeated questioning of his models by management and a formal review of his past bids, which he experienced as a personal attack on his integrity and professional identity. He started poring obsessively over emails, meeting notes, and project data at home, trying to reconcile perceived inconsistencies, and gradually interpreted ordinary managerial oversight and software glitches as evidence of a coordinated effort to undermine or scapegoat him. Over the following year, this fixed interpretation solidified despite colleagues’ reassurances and an overall satisfactory performance review, and after his wife and a trusted coworker noticed how preoccupied and inflexible he had become about these beliefs and how much it was straining his sleep and home life, they persuaded him to see a psychiatrist.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m here because I have these beliefs about what’s going on at work that nobody can talk me out of, no matter what they show me.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: No matter how many times they tell me it’s just routine oversight or a software bug, I can’t shake the conviction that certain managers are quietly manipulating the numbers and project files to make my cost estimates look wrong so they can pin the hospital overruns on me and push me out, and I see signs of it in every oddly timed email, every ‘accidental’ system glitch, even in who gets copied or left off of meeting invites.
